title: Feelings Change and Differ
keyIdea: Everyone has feelings. Feelings change during a day, and big ones pass, often faster with a calm, kind way to cope. The same thing can make two people feel different things, because of what they like and what has happened to them before. Nobody's feeling is wrong, and we can be kind about a feeling we do not share.

kid: You have lots of feelings in one day. Happy at breakfast. Cross when a toy breaks. Calm at bedtime. Feelings come and go.
A big feeling can feel like it will last for ever. It will not. Take slow breaths, hug a teddy or tell a grown-up. The feeling gets smaller.
Two kids can see the same thing and feel two different things. Mia loves dogs. A dog once jumped on Leo. When a dog runs up, Mia smiles and Leo hides.
Nobody has the wrong feeling. If your friend feels sad and you feel happy, you can still be kind. Say, "I see you are sad."
adult: This topic has three ideas: everyone has feelings, feelings change over a day, and the same event can bring out different feelings in different people. Children usually name happy, sad, cross and scared first; here they use those words to track how feelings rise and fall and to explain why a friend reacts differently. It sits in the IB PYP personal, social and physical education strand on identity and in the PSHE Association's early-years and Key Stage 1 work on feelings.

Feelings differ because people bring different likes, memories and needs to the same moment. A child who was knocked over by a dog will feel fear where a dog owner feels joy. Seeing that a feeling has a reason, even if you do not share it, is an early step towards empathy.

Common mistakes: thinking a bad mood will last all day; believing there is one right feeling for an event, so someone who feels differently is wrong or silly; telling someone to stop feeling sad, which does not work; and thinking a person can only feel one thing at a time. Hitting or throwing things when cross also tends to make the feeling bigger.

At bedtime, draw a quick feelings line for the day: a face for the morning, school, play, tea and bed, joined by a line that goes up and down. Talk about what changed each feeling. When siblings react differently to the same thing, ask each of them what made them feel that way.

familyTip: At bedtime, ask "What was one feeling this morning and one feeling now?" If a sibling or friend felt differently about the same thing, ask "Why might they have felt that way?"

practice.prompt: Pip felt cross at breakfast. What will Pip probably feel later in the day?
choices: Pip will be cross all day
Pip will never feel happy again
practice.hint: Think of the mood line in Pip's day. Did it stay in one place?
practice.explain: Feelings change during a day. A cross start does not mean a cross day.

practice.prompt: {n} children see the same big dog. Will they all feel the same?
choices: Not always: they can feel different things
practice.hint: Think of Mia and Leo. Did the same dog make them feel the same?
practice.explain: Each of the {n} children has their own likes and memories, so their feelings can differ.

practice.prompt: Ava is sad the picnic is off. Ben loves rain. What is a kind thing for Ben to say?
choices: I see you are sad. Want to play inside?
practice.hint: Which one shows Ben noticed how Ava feels?
practice.explain: Ben can feel happy and still be kind by saying he sees Ava's sad feeling.

practice.prompt: Max feels very cross. He counts to {n} slowly and tells his dad. What happens to the cross feeling?
practice.hint: Think of Pip's cross cloud. What made it shrink?
practice.explain: Calm ways, like counting to {n} and telling a grown-up, help a big feeling pass.

pool.prompt: What happens to feelings during a day?
choices: We only have one feeling a day
pool.hint: Think of your own day: wake up, school, play, bed.
pool.explain: Feelings change as different things happen during the day.

pool.prompt: Leo is scared of dogs. Mia loves dogs. Who has the wrong feeling?
pool.hint: Do both children have a reason for how they feel?
pool.explain: Nobody is wrong. A dog jumped on Leo once, and Mia has a dog at home.

pool.prompt: Why might two children feel differently about fireworks?
choices: Loud bangs hurt one child's ears, and the other loves the lights
Fireworks make everyone feel the same
pool.hint: Think about what each child likes or has felt before.
pool.explain: Different likes and different past times lead to different feelings.

pool.prompt: Zoe has been cross for {n} minutes. Which helps the feeling pass?
choices: Take slow breaths and tell a grown-up
pool.hint: Which one is calm and does not hurt anyone?
pool.explain: After {n} minutes, slow breaths and talking help. Throwing or shouting makes it bigger.

pool.prompt: Can you feel happy and scared at the same time, like on a big slide?
choices: Yes, you can feel two things at once
No, only one feeling at a time
pool.hint: How do you feel at the top of a big slide?
pool.explain: People can feel more than one thing at once, like happy and scared.

pool.prompt: {n} friends watch a film. Some find it funny and some find it scary. What does this show?
choices: The same thing can make people feel different things
pool.explain: Even with {n} friends watching the same film, each one can feel something different.

pool.prompt: Your friend is sad because she lost the race. You won. What is kind to say?
choices: Good race. Want to run again?
It's only a race, stop being sad.
pool.hint: Which one is kind about her sad feeling?
pool.explain: You can be glad you won and still be kind about her sad feeling.

pool.prompt: Is it OK to have a sad or cross feeling?
choices: Yes, everyone has them, and they pass
No, you must always be happy
pool.hint: Do grown-ups ever feel sad or cross?
pool.explain: All feelings are OK. What matters is a kind, safe way to cope with them.

visual.caption: Your friend feels differently from you. Is it kind or unkind to say? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: You are wrong to feel that.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: fill Pip's day with feelings, see why two children feel differently about the same thing, help a cross feeling pass, and pick kind words.
